Provide a simple per-cpuset metric of memory pressure
that the tasks in a cpuset call try_to_free_pages()
(direct) memory reclaim code.
This enables batch managers monitoring jobs running in dedicated cpusets to
efficiently detect what level of memory pressure that job is causing.
This is useful both on tightly managed systems running a wide mix of
submitted jobs
column2: which may choose to terminate or reprioritize jobs that are

column1: trying to use more memory than allowed on the nodes assigned them
tightly coupled
that will dramatically fail to meet required performance goals if they
start to use more memory than allowed to them.
This patch just provides a very economical way for the batch manager to
monitor a cpuset for signs of memory pressure.  It's up to the batch
manager or other user code to decide what to do about it and take action.
==> Unless this feature is enabled by writing ""1"" to the special file
/dev/cpuset/memory_pressure_enabled
code of __alloc_pages() for this metric reduces to simply noticing
that the cpuset_memory_pressure_enabled flag is zero.  So only
systems that enable this feature will compute the metric.
Why a per-cpuset
Because this meter is per-cpuset
system load imposed by a batch scheduler monitoring this metric is
sharply reduced on large systems
column2: because a scan of the tasklist can be

column1: avoided on each set of queries.
Because this meter is a running average
counter
column2: a batch scheduler can detect memory pressure with a single

column1: read
column2: instead of having to read and accumulate results for a period of

Because this meter is per-cpuset rather than per-task or mm
batch scheduler can obtain the key information
cpuset

column2: and updated by any task attached to that cpuset

column1: enters the synchronous (direct) page reclaim code.

in the cpuset
